desc:
You are given a binary string s. You may apply the following two rewrite rules any number of times, in any order:

  • if s contains "00", replace one occurrence of it by "10";
  • if s contains "10", replace one occurrence of it by "01".

Return the largest string you can reach, comparing strings as binary numbers (all reachable strings have the same length, so this is the same as lexicographic order). Doing nothing is allowed.

For example, "000110" can become "111011", "01" stays "01", and "1100" becomes "1110".
constraints: s contains only the characters '0' and '1'
hints: Leading ones can never be improved, and a string without any zero is already the largest possible. Focus on what happens from the first zero onwards.

The second rule moves a zero one step left past a one (the string gets smaller), but it lets you gather all zeros into one block. The first rule then turns pairs of neighbouring zeros in that block into a one and a zero, which makes the string larger.

Let p be the index of the first zero and z the number of zeros in the whole string. Look at the quantity (index of the first zero) + (number of zeros): no rule can increase it. The best you can reach is a single zero at index p + z - 1, with ones everywhere else.
editorial: If the string has no zero, it is already all ones. Otherwise let p be the index of the first zero and z the total number of zeros in s (all of them sit at or after p). The p characters before the first zero are ones and stay that way.

Construction: use 10 -> 01 to slide every zero left until all z zeros form a block starting at index p, followed only by ones. Then apply 00 -> 10 to the first two zeros of the block, again and again: 0 0 0 -> 1 0 0 -> 1 1 0. After z - 1 applications the block has become z - 1 ones and a single zero, giving '1' * (p + z - 1) + '0' + '1' * (n - p - z).

Why nothing is larger: consider f = (index of the first zero) + (number of zeros). Rule 1 applied at the first zero raises the index by one and removes one zero, so f stays the same; rule 1 anywhere else removes a zero, so f drops; rule 2 never changes the number of zeros and cannot move the first zero to the right, so f does not grow. There is always at least one zero (the rules never remove the last one), so the first zero ends at index at most f - 1 = p + z - 1. The string with ones everywhere except that single zero is the largest possible. Time O(n), space O(n) for the output.
